keyFindings.description: Round 2, finding 1 (the residual of round 1's finding 1, and the question the architect asked me to decide). The per-ask clip is clipBytes, which keeps the head, while rule no_change is defined by the ask's own recommendation, which a written ask carries at or near the end. Whenever the clip fires it removes exactly that sentence. Measured against the exported describeAsks at this head: one 9 KB ask, asksCut 1, recommendation reaches the model in 0 of 1; two 9 KB asks, 0 of 2; thirty 1 KB asks, asksCut 30, 0 of 30; four to twenty asks that fit, asksCut 0, all of them. The call then records ruleOutcome "none" — judged and clean — for an ask whose deciding line the model never saw. The tester's own control measures it from the other side: the same four 9 KB blocks, the same bytes, differing only in where the no-change sentence sits, give match within the per-ask ceiling and none past it. Sharing the list budget made this bite earlier than at the round-1 head: the effective ceiling is now the share (3,226 B at ten asks, 1,588 B at twenty), not 8 KiB, so a spec with a dozen multi-KB ask blocks has every one of them clipped where the first-come version judged the first few whole. Remedy: a sibling of clipBytes that keeps a head and a tail around the elision marker, used by describeAsks alone — rule 1 reads the end, rule 2 reads the start, at the same byte cost. The stale sentences in README.md:343-344, askgate-core.ts:132-133 and :360 (the request may leave an ask out; each ask capped at 8 KiB) go with it.

Round 2, finding 2: the finding-4 fix reopens round 1's finding 1 one level down. When the de-duplication read fails, an upload is narrowed to the openers with no id. If every opener carries an #id — a re-upload of a document downloaded from Dispatch, where every stored block already has one, plus a genuinely new :::ask{#new} the agent wrote — the narrowed list is empty, runRulesCheck returns undefined at :414, the entry gets no ruleOutcome, no ruleAsksCut and no ruleAsksPartial, and decision-record.ts:148 (ruleOutcome === null && !override) writes no record at all. The new ask posts, nobody judged it, and no count says so: askgate-report.ts counts a rules call as a record with ruleOutcome !== null, and the new cut and partial counts live inside that set. ruleAsksPartial was added for exactly this distinction and does not fire in the worse case. The round's own test pins the behaviour (expect(check).toBeUndefined() in "an unchanged document re-uploaded when the de-duplication read fails is not refused"). Remedy: asks.length === 0 is two facts. "This call opens no new ask" is undefined; "the read failed, so the gate judged none of this call's asks" must still return a RulesCheck with asksPartial true and an outcome that does not read as judged-and-clean, with no model call.

Round 2, finding 3: the breaker now counts on the target and passes on the ask, and the two registers disagree. count() counts refusals per target; covers() decides the pass from the union of ask identities that rules refusals named there. (a) An ask refused once is passed on its next send: ask A refused twice on target T leaves count 2; a call opening ask B is reviewed (correct) and refused, which appends B to the union and makes count 3; the next send of B is tripped && covers, so it goes out unreviewed with renderBreakerAck's "Third attempt on this target after two refusals" — B was refused once, and the README, the header comment and that text all promise two. Test 14b sets this up and stops one call short of it. (b) A target whose refusals named an ask never passes a call that opens none: covers is refused.length === 0 || asks.some(...), so once any rules refusal named an ask, a later call opening no new ask (a plain replace edit, a comment) can never be covered, and the termination the breaker exists for is gone for that target, where before the third attempt went out. The documented rule, askgate-core.ts:95-97 and README:291-296, is "a target whose refusals named no ask", which is "this refusal named none", not "no refusal ever named one". One shape fixes both: count refusals per refused thing — one counter keyed target + "" for a whole-call refusal and target + askIdentity for each ask a rules refusal named — and pass a call when its own thing has two. covers(), Revise.asks, the asks.length === ruled.names.length fallback and the asymmetry between the rules-match path and the charter path all fall out.

Round 2, finding 4: an ask block's #id goes into the <ask> open tag verbatim and is charged against the list's budget at :264-270 before any text is clipped, with no bound on its length; new-asks.ts's directiveAttributes imposes none and the server accepts one. Measured at this head on a two-block document, the second block carrying a real recommendation: id 3 chars, list 862 B, asksCut 0, recommendation reaches the model; id 20,000, list 20,859 B, still reaches it; id 32,000, list 32,759 B, asksCut 1, it does not; id 64,000, list 64,126 B, asksCut 2, it does not. Confirmed against the real parser that the server creates both asks for a 32,000-character id (pmdoc.Parse and pmdoc.ParseFragment both answer 2, no error), so the write is not refused for it. Two consequences: one block empties every other ask's body in the same call, so no rule can fire for any of them, and the 32 KiB bound the module documents does not hold at all — the list reached 64 KB. describeAsks's own new comment says a call would need hundreds of asks to exceed the bound on tags; one block does. Remedy: clip the id where the tag is built and give each ask's text a floor, so the tags can never take the whole list.

The refusal path maps the model's ask numbers onto a second, independent parse: matches[].ask numbers the asks runRulesCheck built from its own newAsks(call.toolName, call.input), and the core re-parses the same arguments with callAsks() and indexes its array with those numbers, guarding the contract with asks.length === ruled.names.length and inventing a third behaviour when it does not hold. RulesCheck already holds the list it judged; returning it removes the length guard, the fallback and the second parse.

clipBytes reserves 32 bytes for its marker, so a budget under 32 emits a marker larger than the budget: describeAsks can overshoot ASKS_MAX_BYTES by about 24 bytes per ask. Returning an empty body below the marker size would make the bound hold.

asksCut's reworded doc ("each clipped ask, counted once") contradicts :274, which still counts every textMissing ask, whose placeholder body is complete and whose own field is ruleTextMissing. Also, asksCut counts asks and not elided bytes, so the report's new line cannot tell an ask clipped by 34 bytes from one clipped to nothing — a difference that matters for finding 1.

askIdentity keys a non-retype ask on the first 60 code points of its text, so two asks sharing an opening share a breaker identity and one pass can cover the other. Also askgate-report.ts now refuses --dispatch-project '' but still accepts --sessions ''.

notes: CI read on GitHub, not from a handoff: main's rulesets require lint, typecheck, test and pr-title (branch protection names none); the branch's newest pull_request run is at 58cf263e4b6fa6d28e937712b2b0ccaf5a548888; all four are completed and success there (one earlier pr-title run was cancelled and is superseded by nine successes); compare 58cf263e...0b0f75db lists only .legion/ paths. The non-required Legion Envoy and Contracts, Docs and Worker Image lanes were still running at the read.

Round 1's four findings: finding 3 (footnote definitions) is closed and accepted — I rebuilt the Go/TS differential at this head (a harness calling pmdoc.Parse and pmdoc.ParseFragment against askBlocks and newAsks) over 6,033 documents, 3,935 fragment and 4,387 whole-document comparisons over the rows the server accepts, 0 divergences, and my round-1 minimal reproducer now agrees on both sides; the shared insert table grew from 13 to 18 rows with five footnote cases, which binds the Go server test and new-asks.test.ts to the same answer. Findings 1, 2 and 4 are closed in the case reported and each left a new defect in its replacement, which are round 2's findings 1, 3 and 2. Thread PRRT_kwDORFy7ds6v-tYI is accepted and left resolved; PRRT_kwDORFy7ds6v-tYF, -tYH and -tYJ were answered again and unresolved.

The architect asked me to decide whether the head-only clip is a correctness gap or a risk line. It is a gap: the clip removes the sentence the rule is defined by, 100% of the times it fires, and the budget sharing this round added made it fire earlier. Both thermonuclear agents reached the same conclusion independently, and the tester's own companion run is the control.

Both thermonuclear agents ran at the reviewed head and returned CHANGES. Their differentials (25,412 and 26,000 compared rows, 0 divergences; 406 and 3,379 when the footnote fix is reverted) agree with mine. Findings 1 to 4 are each re-verified here before being written: findings 1 and 4 by running describeAsks at this head, finding 2 and finding 3 by the control flow in rules-check.ts:321/:414 with decision-record.ts:148 and in askgate-core.ts:1994-2011 with :2474 and :2590.

Checked and clean this round: the warn-mode counting is fixed (refused is set only in block mode at :2667, a rules match returns block: true in either mode and always counts); renderWarn no longer promises an unreviewed third resend; revisesForKey keeps its meaning through the new revises(); ruleTextMissing is no longer set when no ask lost its text; ruleAsksPartial is plumbed entry → record → report; PLUGIN now reads pkg.name, whose value is byte-identical to the string it replaced, so no record's plugin value moves; --dispatch-project '' is refused by name; the 17,000 ms minimum is documented in README, AGENTS.md and CHANGELOG and matches MIN_DEADLINE_MS plus CEILING_MARGIN_MS, and the tester drove 16,000 and 17,000 live. Every fix carries a regression test; 119 targeted tests pass here and the pair measured 327 across the four files.
